items.new: Now this ambergris is a very curious substance, and it was so important as an article of trade that in 1791 a certain Nantucket-born Captain Coffin was questioned about it at the bar of the English House of Commons. At that time, and in fact until fairly recently, the exact origin of ambergris was, like that of amber itself, a puzzle to scholars. The word ambergris is simply the French compound for "gray amber," yet the two substances are entirely different. Amber is sometimes found on the seashore, but it is also dug up from soil far inland, whereas ambergris is found only at sea. Amber, moreover, is hard, transparent, brittle and odorless, and it is used for pipe mouthpieces, beads and ornaments. Ambergris is soft and waxy, and so intensely fragrant and spicy that it is widely used in perfume, in pastilles, fine candles, hair powders and pomade. The Turks cook with it, and they also carry it to Mecca for the same purpose that frankincense is carried to St. Peter's in Rome. Some wine merchants drop a few grains into claret to flavor it.

items.new: The try-works stand between the foremast and the mainmast, where the deck has the most room. The timbers underneath are specially strong, built to carry the weight of an almost solid block of brick and mortar about ten feet by eight and five feet high. The foundation does not go through the deck; instead, the masonry is bolted firmly to the surface by heavy iron knees that brace it on every side and screw it down to the timbers. Its sides are cased in wood, and its top is completely covered by a large, sloping, battened hatch. Take off this hatch and you uncover the great try-pots. There are two of them, and each holds several barrels. When they are not in use, they are kept remarkably clean. Sometimes they are polished with soapstone and sand until the insides shine like silver punch-bowls. On night watches some cynical old sailors will crawl into them and curl up there for a nap. While the pots are being polished — one man in each, side by side — plenty of confidential talk passes back and forth over the iron rims. It is also a place for deep mathematical thought. It was in the Pequod's left-hand try-pot, with the soapstone busily circling around me, that the remarkable fact first struck me, indirectly, that in geometry all bodies sliding along the cycloid, my soapstone for example, will descend from any point in exactly the same time.

On it stood the Tartarean shapes of the pagan harpooners, who are always the stokers on a whale-ship. With huge pronged poles they tossed hissing masses of blubber into the scalding pots or stirred up the fires underneath, until the flames shot out of the doors like curling snakes and snapped at their feet. The smoke rolled away in sullen heaps. Every time the ship pitched, the boiling oil pitched with her, as if it longed to leap into their faces. Across from the mouth of the works, on the far side of the wide wooden hearth, was the windlass, which served as a sea-going sofa. The watch lounged there when they had nothing else to do, staring into the red heat of the fire until their eyes felt scorched in their heads. Their tawny faces, now thick with grime from smoke and sweat, their matted beards, and by contrast the barbaric brilliance of their teeth were all strangely lit up by the flickering blaze of the works. As they told each other their unholy adventures, tales of terror in words of mirth; as their wild laughter forked up out of them like the flames from the furnace; as the harpooners gestured wildly back and forth in front of them with their huge pronged forks and dippers; as the wind howled on, and the sea leaped, and the ship groaned and dove, and still kept driving her red hell farther and farther into the blackness of the sea and the night, and scornfully champed the white bone in her mouth, and spat viciously all around her; then the rushing Pequod, loaded with savages and freighted with fire, burning a corpse and plunging into that blackness of darkness, seemed the physical counterpart of her monomaniac commander's soul.

items.new: But that night in particular something strange happened to me, something I have never been able to explain. I jerked awake from a brief sleep on my feet, horribly aware that something was fatally wrong. The jawbone tiller was hitting my side, where I had been leaning against it; in my ears was the low hum of sails just starting to shake in the wind. I thought my eyes were open, and I was half aware of putting my fingers to the lids and mechanically stretching them even wider. Yet in spite of all this I could see no compass in front of me to steer by, though it seemed only a minute since I had been watching the card in the light of the steady binnacle lamp. There seemed to be nothing ahead of me but a jet-black gloom, made ghastly now and then by flashes of red. My strongest impression was that whatever swift, rushing thing I was standing on was not so much heading for any harbor ahead as fleeing from every harbor behind. A stark, bewildered feeling, like death, came over me. My hands clutched the tiller convulsively, but with the crazy idea that the tiller had somehow, by some enchantment, been turned upside down. My God! What is the matter with me? I thought. And then I saw it: in my brief sleep I had turned around and was facing the ship's stern, with my back to her bow and the compass. In an instant I turned back, just in time to keep the vessel from flying up into the wind and very likely capsizing. How glad and how grateful I was to be free of this unnatural hallucination of the night, and of the fatal danger of being brought by the lee!
